blocks.quote: RNNs propagate information **step by step**, a signal from token 1 to token 50 must survive 49 sequential multiplications. If the weight matrix has spectral radius $< 1$, the signal decays exponentially:
blocks.section: Long Distance Dependencies

blocks.quote: Self-attention bypasses this entirely. In bidirectional self-attention every token attends to every other in **one step**; a causal decoder lets each token attend only to itself and the past:
blocks.section: Long Distance Dependencies

blocks.quote: The score has no explicit distance term, and that is not an accident but a symmetry: self-attention is **permutation-equivariant**. Shuffle the input tokens and each output moves with its own token, because the layer sees the sequence as a set and has no built-in notion of order. Word order must therefore be injected separately. The original Transformer added fixed sinusoidal or learned absolute position embeddings (\cite[Vaswani et al., 2017]{vaswani2017attention}); later models moved to relative schemes. **Rotary position embedding (RoPE)** rotates each query and key by an angle proportional to its position, so their dot product depends only on the *offset* between the two tokens, and it became the default in open-weight models such as the Llama line (\cite[Su et al., 2021]{su2021rope}); **ALiBi** instead subtracts a linear penalty proportional to distance from the scores, which improves extrapolation to sequences longer than those seen in training (\cite[Press et al., 2022]{press2022alibi}). Because RoPE puts position in through a rotation, methods that rescale or interpolate those frequencies can stretch a pretrained model's usable context with only modest fine-tuning (\cite[Peng et al., 2023]{peng2023yarn}). In an encoder, token 1 can attend to token 500 as directly as to token 2; in a causal decoder, token 500 can attend back to token 1 as directly as to token 499.

blocks.quote: In a Transformer model, words don't live in a dictionary; they live in a **Semantic Universe**. Every concept, from “apple” to “existentialism”, is assigned a specific coordinate in a high-dimensional map. However, some words suffer from a serious identity crisis.
blocks.section: Long Distance Dependencies

blocks.quote: Even though in this example, we treat tokens as words, they can also be parts of words or single characters like a comma or a semicolon due to *Byte-Pair-Encodings*, invented by \citeauthor{gage1994bpe} as a **data-compression** algorithm in \citeyear{gage1994bpe} \cite{gage1994bpe}. The compression idea is what produces the subwords: each merge fuses the most frequent adjacent pair into a single new symbol — a **short ID that stands in for a longer string** — so frequent patterns get short codes, rare ones long, and the resulting token stream is usually a shorter, lossless form of the original text.
blocks.section: Long Distance Dependencies

blocks.quote: In the history of linguistics, \citeauthor{zelligharris}'s \citeyear{zelligharris} paper on distributional structure (\cite[Harris, 1954]{zelligharris}) and \citeauthor{firth1957distributive}'s \citeyear{firth1957distributive} maxim, “You shall know a word by the company it keeps”, both suggest that words occurring in similar contexts share similar meanings. This shift away from fixed dictionary definitions to context-based identity allowed later researchers like \citeauthor{mikolov2013word2vec} (\citeyear{mikolov2013word2vec}) to mathematically map language into the vector spaces we see in modern LLMs today.
blocks.section: Long Distance Dependencies

blocks.quote: Attention entered neural machine translation as a fix for a bottleneck. \citeauthor{bahdanau2014} paired an encoder that compressed a source sentence into a single fixed-length vector with a decoder that *looked back* at every encoder state, weighting them by a learned alignment score (\cite[Bahdanau et al., 2014]{bahdanau2014}). The weights came from a small feed-forward network — **additive attention** — and were trained end-to-end with the translation objective. The result was better translation on long sentences and a readable alignment map: the model had learned *which source words to consult* for each output word.
blocks.section: Long Distance Dependencies

blocks.quote: The step from cross-sequence attention to attention *within* one sequence came earlier than the Transformer. In January 2016, \citeauthor{cheng2016} used what they called **intra-attention** to let a memory-augmented LSTM relate each word to its predecessors while reading (\cite[Cheng et al., 2016]{cheng2016}). Five months later, \citeauthor{parikh2016} built a model almost entirely out of attention — with optional intra-sentence attention and no recurrence over word order — and matched far heavier recurrent models on natural language inference (\cite[Parikh et al., 2016]{parikh2016}). In March 2017, \citeauthor{lin2017selfattentive} ran multiple attention heads over an LSTM and extracted an interpretable sentence embedding from them (\cite[Lin et al., 2017]{lin2017selfattentive}). The ingredients were in place; what was missing was the willingness to drop the recurrent scaffold entirely.
blocks.section: Long Distance Dependencies

blocks.quote: The decisive step was to delete the recurrence altogether. \citeauthor{vaswani2017attention} replaced the LSTM encoder–decoder with **self-attention**: every position forms its own query, key, and value, and every position attends to every other in one layer (\cite[Vaswani et al., 2017]{vaswani2017attention}). Recurrence had forced the model to carry information through a chain of hidden states; self-attention made the path between any two positions length one. The cost was quadratic in sequence length; the benefit was parallel training and direct long-range access. The same layer, stacked, became the Transformer.
blocks.section: Long Distance Dependencies

blocks.section: Summary: Why *That* Equation?

blocks.quote: 3. **Softmax**: Turns raw scores into a **probability distribution**, non-negative weights that sum to 1. This means the output is a **convex combination** of values, geometrically trapped inside their convex hull. It's the minimal assumption: “blend the available information proportionally to relevance.”
blocks.section: Summary: Why *That* Equation?

blocks.quote: 4. **Weighted sum of Values**: The output is an interpolation, not a lookup. This is differentiable everywhere, enabling gradient-based learning. The FFN layer that follows provides the non-linearity needed to “escape” the convex hull and create genuinely new representations.
blocks.section: Summary: Why *That* Equation?

blocks.quote: There is a third reading of the same equation, from kernel methods. If you treat the softmax weights as a **kernel** over keys, attention can be read as **Nadaraya–Watson kernel smoothing**: the output at a query is a weighted average of the values, with weights that fall off as the query and key diverge (\cite[Tsai et al., 2019]{tsai2019kernel}). The dot product plays the role of the kernel’s similarity function, the softmax its normalization, and the value vectors the observations being smoothed. This view explains why attention is a *local* averaging operation in representation space — and why it cannot, by itself, create a representation outside the convex hull of its values.
blocks.section: Summary: Why *That* Equation?

blocks.quote: The Physics of the “Handshake”
blocks.section: The Physics of the “Handshake”

blocks.quote: To decide how much “pull” one word has on another, the model performs a mathematical handshake using three specific projections:
blocks.section: The Physics of the “Handshake”

blocks.quote: 1. **Query ($\mathbf{q}$):** The word looking for context (e.g., “What kind of Bank am I?”).
blocks.section: The Physics of the “Handshake”

blocks.quote: 2. **Key ($\mathbf{k}$):** The words offering context (e.g., “I am a River, I have water and banks.”).
blocks.section: The Physics of the “Handshake”

blocks.quote: 3. **Value ($\mathbf{v}$):** The actual semantic “content” to be shared.
blocks.section: The Physics of the “Handshake”

blocks.quote: Read the three roles together, and the mechanism stops looking like a lookup keyed by position. The query encodes *what this position is looking for*, the key *what every position advertises*, and the value *what it hands over if chosen*. The dot product $\mathbf{q}_i \cdot \mathbf{k}_j$ is large exactly when those two descriptions match, so attention retrieves by **content rather than by location**: the same learned projections can implement coreference, subject–verb agreement, or bracket matching with no built-in receptive field. That is the sense in which the layer acts as a **content-addressable memory** (\cite[Vaswani et al., 2017]{vaswani2017attention}).
blocks.section: The Physics of the “Handshake”

blocks.quote: The model calculates an alignment score using the scaled dot product:

blocks.quote: The $\sqrt{d_k}$ term is critical, without it, the dot-product magnitudes scale with the head dimension and the softmax saturates. If the Query and Key point in a similar direction, the connection is strong.
blocks.section: The Physics of the “Handshake”

blocks.quote: In modern NLP, words are not merely strings; they are high-dimensional vectors. **Self-Attention** is the operation that allows a model to dynamically re-weight these vectors based on their contextual relevance to one another.

blocks.quote: Multi-Head Attention: Many Lenses at Once
blocks.section: Multi-Head Attention: Many Lenses at Once

blocks.quote: Multi-head attention is not just redundancy. \citeauthor{analyzingmultiheads} found that a small number of heads do most of the work — some track syntactic relations, some attend to rare tokens — and that many heads can be pruned with little loss (\cite[Voita et al., 2019]{analyzingmultiheads}). \citeauthor{michel2019sixteen} asked the bluntest version of the question — whether sixteen heads are really better than one — and found that a large fraction of heads in trained translation and BERT models can be pruned at test time with negligible loss, with some layers collapsing to a single head (\cite[Michel et al., 2019]{michel2019sixteen}). \citeauthor{htu2019dependencies} showed that individual BERT heads specialize in particular dependency types, though no single head is a clean parser (\cite[Htut et al., 2019]{htu2019dependencies}). \citeauthor{clark2019bertattention} added a blunter finding: much BERT attention lands on `[SEP]`, `[CLS]`, and punctuation, so a raw attention map is a weak explanation of what the model computes (\cite[Clark et al., 2019]{clark2019bertattention}). \citeauthor{jain2019attention} pushed the point further: attention weights often fail standard tests for explanation, because alternative weightings can yield identical predictions and different attention distributions can produce the same output (\cite[Jain & Wallace, 2019]{jain2019attention}). The working consensus is that a raw attention map is **suggestive rather than faithful** — one probe among many, not a proof of what the network computed.
blocks.section: Multi-Head Attention: Many Lenses at Once

blocks.quote: Other extensions change how heads interact rather than how many there are: **talking-heads attention** inserts learned linear mixing across heads before and after the softmax (\cite[Shazeer et al., 2020]{shazeer2020talkingheads}), letting a head condition its attention on what its neighbours are doing.

blocks.quote: A Simple Picture: Attention Is Moving Sand
blocks.section: A Simple Picture: Attention Is Moving Sand

blocks.quote: Imagine you have exactly **one bucket of attention** to hand out. The **keys** are places that can take some of it. Sending attention to a key that is very similar to the query is cheap; sending it to a very different key is expensive. So you naturally want to send the sand where it is cheap.
blocks.section: A Simple Picture: Attention Is Moving Sand

blocks.quote: But there is a catch. If you pour the whole bucket onto the single cheapest key, you commit completely. A tiny difference in similarity then decides everything, and the model stops listening to the other keys. To stay flexible, you also want to spread some sand around. These two wishes pull in opposite directions:
blocks.section: A Simple Picture: Attention Is Moving Sand

blocks.quote: - **Cheap:** put the mass on the most similar key.
blocks.section: A Simple Picture: Attention Is Moving Sand

blocks.quote: - **Spread out:** do not put all your eggs in one basket.

blocks.quote: Why the temperature is $\sqrt{d_k}$
blocks.section: Why the temperature is $\sqrt{d_k}$

blocks.quote: A dot product grows with the number of dimensions. If the components of the query and key vectors are independent and of typical size $1$, their dot product is typically of size $\sqrt{d_k}$. Without scaling, a wider model would automatically have larger scores, the softmax would become sharp, and small differences would turn into near-certain decisions. Dividing the score by $\sqrt{d_k}$ keeps the temperature in a useful range, so the compromise between cheap and spread stays meaningful (\cite[Litman, 2025]{litman2025sdpaot}).
blocks.section: Why the temperature is $\sqrt{d_k}$

blocks.quote: Where the sand picture comes from
blocks.section: Where the sand picture comes from

blocks.quote: Moving a fixed amount of mass from places of supply to places of demand at minimum cost is an old problem called **optimal transport**. In the classical version there are many sources and many destinations, and both amounts are fixed. Here there is only **one source** — the query, with one unit of attention mass — and the destinations have no required amount. That is the "one-sided" in the paper's title. With only one constraint, the best plan has a direct formula; no iterative algorithm is needed. When both sides are fixed, the usual method is the Sinkhorn iteration (\cite[Cuturi, 2013]{cuturi2013sinkhorn}), which repeats row and column normalizations. Attention fixes only the rows, so it gets the closed form for free.
blocks.section: Where the sand picture comes from

blocks.quote: The whole story in three sentences
blocks.section: The whole story in three sentences

blocks.quote: The **forward pass** solves a precise problem: spread one unit of attention so that it is cheap and still flexible. Its unique answer is the softmax you already know. The **backward pass** then turns the loss into a reward signal and moves attention toward keys that beat the current average. The same geometry governs both halves, which is why the formula and its learning rule fit together so neatly.
blocks.section: The whole story in three sentences

blocks.quote: What the paper does **not** claim: it does not add a new attention mechanism, it does not report experiments, and it does not replace softmax with Sinkhorn. It is an explanation of the mechanism we already have. The link between spreading and entropy is classical (\cite[Jaynes, 1957]{jaynes1957maxent}); what is new is the transport framing, the advantage-based reading of the gradient, and the geometric bridge between them.
blocks.section: The whole story in three sentences

blocks.quote: A hidden identity: the softmax is the Sinkhorn iteration
blocks.section: A hidden identity: the softmax is the Sinkhorn iteration

blocks.quote: So a single attention layer is quietly instantiating a problem with a long history in analysis. Each query's attention — a row of unit probability mass spread over the whole sequence — is a soft **transport plan**: the most "spread out" (maximum-entropy) assignment of that query's attention to the keys that is still consistent with their scores. This is why the $\sqrt{d_k}$ scaling and the softmax feel so load-bearing: they keep the "transport" well-conditioned, for exactly the reason the entropic regularization keeps the Sinkhorn iteration stable.
blocks.section: A hidden identity: the softmax is the Sinkhorn iteration

blocks.quote: The analogy above is actually a theorem, in a degenerate one-sided version of the problem. **The attention row of a single query is the exact, closed-form solution to a *one-sided* entropic optimal transport problem** (\cite[Litman, 2025]{litman2025sdpaot}): the query is a single unit of attention mass (a point source), there is no target marginal to match, and the only question is how to spread that mass over the keys. The problem asks for the distribution that *maximizes the expected similarity* to the query while being *maximally entropic*, with the temperature $\tau$ (the $\sqrt{d_k}$ above) as the entropic regularization strength — and the unique solution of that strictly convex problem is precisely the softmax. The forward pass is therefore not a heuristic "differentiable argmax" but **optimal inference**: the answer to a well-posed variational problem.
blocks.section: A hidden identity: the softmax is the Sinkhorn iteration

blocks.section: Keeping it Fair (The Scaling & Softmax)

blocks.quote: We don't just use the raw scores because they can get too huge to handle, making the model “stubborn.” We use two steps to clean them up:

blocks.quote: This forces all the attention for a single word to add up to exactly **100%**. If a word gives 85% of its focus to one neighbor, it only has 15% left to split among everyone else.

blocks.quote: Summary: The Vector Tug-of-War
blocks.section: Summary: The Vector Tug-of-War

blocks.quote: In the world of Transformers, meaning is **movement**. Instead of looking up a word in a static dictionary, the model calculates a new position for that word based on the “gravitational pull” of its neighbours in the embedding space. This creates a vector that is near the *meaning* of the word in the context it is used in, not the mere embedding of the word itself.
blocks.section: Summary: The Vector Tug-of-War

blocks.quote: The classic illustration: the word **“apple”** is ambiguous in isolation, but in *I ate a juicy apple* the word **“juicy”** pulls the apple vector toward the fruit cluster, the same dot-product mechanism this page demonstrates geometrically with the step-by-step walkthrough above.
blocks.section: Summary: The Vector Tug-of-War

blocks.quote: Attention Heads as Differentiable Turing Machine Read Heads
blocks.section: Attention Heads as Differentiable Turing Machine Read Heads

blocks.quote: In \citeyear{neuralturingmachines}, the concept of Neural Turing Machine (NTM) was introduced by \citeauthorlastnameand{neuralturingmachines}, demonstrating that a neural network coupled with an external memory and differentiable read/write heads could learn algorithms end-to-end via gradient descent. The critical mechanism enabling this was an *attentional process* over memory locations, the read head produces a weighting vector with one component per memory cell, determining what to retrieve.
blocks.section: Attention Heads as Differentiable Turing Machine Read Heads

blocks.quote: This explains both why Transformers can learn algorithmic tasks (sorting, addition, in-context learning) and why they sometimes fail: the read heads emit *soft*, probabilistic weightings via softmax, meaning they can approximate but never perfectly execute the discrete, hard-addressed steps a classical Turing machine performs.
blocks.section: Attention Heads as Differentiable Turing Machine Read Heads

blocks.quote: Attention as Retrieval-Augmented Memory
blocks.section: Attention as Retrieval-Augmented Memory

blocks.quote: The attention mechanism can be understood as a **differentiable database lookup**. The Query is the search query, the Keys form the index, and the Values are the stored records. This perspective reveals deep connections to several practical systems:
blocks.section: Attention as Retrieval-Augmented Memory

blocks.quote: The Context Window: The Model's Short-Term Memory
blocks.section: The Context Window: The Model's Short-Term Memory

blocks.quote: The **context window** defines the maximum number of tokens a Transformer can “see” and reason about in a single forward pass. It is, in effect, the model's field of vision: any token that falls within the window can participate in the attention mechanism, while anything outside it simply does not exist to the model. Because the self-attention matrix has dimensions $\text{Context} \times \text{Context}$, both memory consumption and computation scale **quadratically** with the window size, doubling the context quadruples the cost. This is the fundamental engineering constraint that prevents context windows from being infinitely large.
blocks.section: The Context Window: The Model's Short-Term Memory

blocks.quote: But the context window is more than a technical parameter, it maps onto a powerful cognitive analogy. The **weights** of the model are its **long-term memory**: everything the model learned during training is crystallized into these fixed parameters, and they do not change during inference. The **context window**, by contrast, is the model's **working memory** or **short-term memory**: it is constructed fresh for every conversation, holds only what has been provided in the current prompt, and is entirely volatile. This maps directly to the psychological distinction between **declarative memory** (stable, accumulated knowledge) and **working memory** (temporary, capacity-limited, actively maintained). When the context window overflows, when a conversation or document exceeds the token limit, the model experiences something analogous to **cognitive overload**: it literally cannot hold all the information simultaneously, and earlier tokens are dropped or truncated. The deeper implication is striking: an LLM has **amnesia between conversations** (no persistent short-term memory carries over) and a **frozen worldview** (no weight updates occur during inference). Every interaction begins from the same fixed long-term knowledge, with no recollection of yesterday. It is, in a sense, like speaking to someone who wakes up every morning with the same education but no memory of any previous conversation.

blocks.section: The Bottom Line

blocks.quote: It is important to note that attention does not only disambiguate words with multiple meanings like “bank” or “apple.” It operates over **every token in the sequence**, refining **all** representations simultaneously. A word like “the” gets contextualized just as much as “bank” does, attention captures syntactic relationships (subject-verb agreement), coreference (linking “she” to “Maria”), temporal reasoning (“before” relating two events), adjectival binding (“red” attaching to “car” rather than “house”), and countless other structural dependencies. The disambiguation examples above are simply the most *visually dramatic* illustration of what is, in reality, a universal mechanism: every word's representation is reshaped by every other word it attends to, regardless of whether the word is ambiguous in isolation.

blocks.quote: The Attention Matrix: A Zero-Sum Economy
blocks.section: The Attention Matrix: A Zero-Sum Economy

blocks.quote: Each row of the attention matrix sums to 1 (due to softmax), making it **right-stochastic**. But the columns generally do **not** sum to 1. This asymmetry reveals something profound: some tokens are “attended to” much more than others, they become **information hubs**.
blocks.section: The Attention Matrix: A Zero-Sum Economy

blocks.quote: In BERT, attention concentrates on the special `[CLS]` and especially `[SEP]` tokens — early heads favour `[CLS]`, middle heads `[SEP]` — which act as sinks rather than content carriers (\cite[Clark et al., 2019]{clark2019bertattention}). In GPT-style models, the first (earliest) token plays a similar role. These tokens become gravitational centers that the entire sequence orbits around.
blocks.section: The Attention Matrix: A Zero-Sum Economy

blocks.quote: The zero-sum nature of attention (each row sums to exactly 1) means attention is a **finite resource**. When one token receives more attention from a given query, every other token necessarily receives less. This is not a design choice, it is a mathematical consequence of the softmax normalization. It creates a competitive economy within every forward pass: tokens compete for attention the way organisms compete for resources in an ecosystem. A highly salient token (a proper noun, a negation word) can “starve” surrounding tokens of attention, causing the model to effectively ignore them.
blocks.section: The Attention Matrix: A Zero-Sum Economy

blocks.quote: The deeper implication: the model cannot attend to everything equally, it must always choose, and every choice is a sacrifice. This mirrors the human condition of finite attention: we cannot listen to all voices simultaneously, and every act of focus is an act of exclusion.
blocks.section: The Attention Matrix: A Zero-Sum Economy

blocks.quote: Why the First Token Steals the Attention: Attention Sinks
blocks.section: Why the First Token Steals the Attention: Attention Sinks

blocks.quote: The zero-sum economy above has a striking corner case that looks like a bug but turns out to be load-bearing. In many trained decoder-only LLMs, a large share of attention mass flows to the **very first token** of the sequence — the `<BOS>` token, or simply the first space — even when that token carries essentially no content. A model reading the 400th word of a paragraph still dumps a meaningful fraction of its attention budget onto word zero. This is the **attention sink**.
blocks.section: Why the First Token Steals the Attention: Attention Sinks

blocks.quote: Why would a model do this? The mechanism is a consequence of the very softmax we derived. Softmax must output a distribution that sums to exactly 1 over every key the query can see. When a query has **no meaningful target** — when the truly relevant tokens are far away, or the context is thin — the model still has to place that leftover probability somewhere. Rather than smear it uniformly, the network learns to route the spare mass to a **designated default**: the earliest token, which is the only key that is *always present, always in-window, and always a valid target* from the very first step of training. Over billions of examples, the first token becomes a neutral "register" — a place where attention parks the mass it has no use for. Remove it, and that mass has nowhere to go, so the whole distribution distorts.
blocks.section: Why the First Token Steals the Attention: Attention Sinks

blocks.quote: This is exactly the trained limit of the $\tfrac{1}{n}$ uniform diagonal you saw earlier. An untrained model spreads attention evenly ($\tfrac{1}{n}$ per token); training sharpens attention onto the tokens that matter — *except* for the residual mass, which retreats to the one position that is guaranteed to be there: the beginning. The first token is where "not-yet-decided" attention goes. The same phenomenon shows up in vision transformers, which grow dedicated **register** tokens that absorb attention and stray artifacts in exactly the same way (\cite[Darcet et al., 2024]{darcet2024registers}) — the architecture needs a drain, so it invents one.
blocks.section: Why the First Token Steals the Attention: Attention Sinks

blocks.quote: The practical upshot is why "infinite" context is not as hard as it sounds: you do not need to remember the whole history, only the sink plus the recent window. But it also means naive "drop the old tokens" memory management silently breaks a model that was never designed to lose its drain.
blocks.section: Why the First Token Steals the Attention: Attention Sinks

blocks.quote: The mechanism behind the sink: working memory, a dark-signal bus, and MLPs that build it
blocks.section: The mechanism behind the sink: working memory, a dark-signal bus, and MLPs that build it

blocks.quote: The "park the leftover mass somewhere" story above is the intuition; three independent mechanistic studies now pin down *why* it works, and they agree. **First, the sink is working memory the network had to build itself.** A Transformer has no persistent state, so it needs somewhere to hold in-progress computation; in vision transformers the model repurposes a few low-information background tokens — or, better, a handful of dedicated empty **register** tokens — as a scratchpad. These outlier tokens provably carry *less* of their local content (position, pixel) than ordinary tokens: they have been **freed for internal computation**, and handing the model four explicit register tokens erases the artifacts entirely (\cite[Darcet et al., 2024]{darcet2024registers}). The "drain" is really a self-provisioned cache. **Second, the sink is a signal bus, not a drain.** Projecting intermediate layers back onto the vocabulary and splitting the embedding spectrum into bands shows that the **low-frequency tail** of the spectrum is exactly what the sink carries: you can suppress large chunks of that spectrum and keep the loss low *only as long as the sink is preserved*, and the tokens that many tokens attend to have their mass concentrated on the tail (\cite[Cancedda, 2024]{cancedda2024sinks}). So the "leftover" mass the softmax must place is not noise; it is the channel through which global, low-frequency structure flows. **Third, the sink is built by identifiable circuits.** Specific middle-layer MLPs actively **synthesize the sink vector** — they map token representations onto the primary sink's direction — and that vector's $\ell_2$-norm sets both how strong the sink is and how many layers it lasts (\cite[Wong et al., 2025]{wong2025sinks}). The sink, in short, is not an accident of initialization: it is manufactured by specific components, which is also why its location and lifetime differ from model to model.
